cultural.vision_reason: This is a strip-woven indigo cotton man's gown (riga/boubou style) with embroidered pocket motifs, a widespread West African Islamic dress tradition also worn among the Wolof; nothing contradicts the claim, though the style is shared across many West African peoples (Hausa, Yoruba, Mande) and cannot distinguish Wolof specifically.

physical.title: tobe; gown
physical.summary: Man's gown (tobe, boubou, riga), composed of 250 narrow strips of hand-spun and hand-woven cotton, hand-sewn together along the selvedges. The strips of the trunk are sewn vertically, and are folded so that the skirt flares out towards the bottom. The strips of the sleeves are horizontally sewn, and those above are longer than those below. The strips are formed in the same way, using alternating threads of indigo-dyed blue and white cotton, giving an effect of a blue/grey (called by the Yoruba 'etu'). A large pocket made of the same fabric has been sewn onto the front of the body. On top of this has been hand-embroidered a design in the 'two knives' pattern in white cotton thread in chain and buttonhole stitch. These cover the pocket, the shoulders, and the large spiral on the back. The hem is lined with a hand-woven cloth of European orange and white cotton in stripes.
